raw_response.headline_result_summary: In cross-sectional OLS regressions with White robust standard errors across 391 municipalities in Minas Gerais, Brazil (Table 4, PDF p. 23), institutional capacity shows mixed effects across its four PCA-derived dimensions: Financial capacity, Technical staffing capacity, and Operational capacity are all positively and significantly associated (p <= 0.013) with both municipal water supply coverage (Atend_Agua: β = 6.015, p = 0.000; β = 2.669, p = 0.007; β = 2.412, p = 0.009) and sanitary sewage coverage (Atend_Esgoto: β = 7.359, p = 0.000; β = 3.941, p = 0.013; β = 13.068, p = 0.000), whereas Political/statutory-planning capacity (having a Municipal Basic Sanitation Plan [PMSB] and Policy [PPSB] under Law 11.445/2007) is significantly negatively associated with water supply coverage (β = -1.890, p = 0.033) and has a statistically null association with sanitary sewage coverage (β = -0.661, p = 0.687). For household solid waste collection (Atend_RDO), Financial (β = 10.064, p = 0.000) and Operational (β = 28.260, p = 0.000) capacities are positive at p < 0.01, while Technical (β = 2.249, p = 0.078) and Political (β = 2.555, p = 0.055) capacities are statistically non-significant at p < 0.05 (significant only at the 10% level). Chi-square and ANOVA tests (p < 0.05) also show that smaller municipalities are significantly less likely to have adopted statutory sanitation plans/policies and have lower per-capita revenues.
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Multi-dimensional exposure split (Administrative/Resource Capacity vs. Statutory Planning Mandate): There is no single composite index of institutional capacity. If a review codes administrative/technical/financial capacity (Capacidade_Financeira, Capacidade_Tecnica, Capacidade_Operacional), all 6 water and sewerage estimates are positive and significant at p < 0.05 (favorable_to_access), matching the authors' abstract summary. Conversely, if a review specifically isolates the legal/regulatory planning factor (Capacidade_Politica, composed of PMSB and PPSB adoption under Law 11.445/2007), the estimate is negative and significant for water coverage (β = -1.890, p = 0.033) and null for sewage coverage (β = -0.661, p = 0.687). 2. Reverse causality / cross-sectional endogeneity: Data are purely cross-sectional (2018 SNIS / 2017 IBGE); the authors explicitly warn that the negative coefficient on Capacidade_Politica for water supply likely reflects low-coverage municipalities only recently adopting municipal plans to qualify for federal funds, and that Capacidade_Financeira includes per-capita water/sewage revenues and expenditures which are mechanically endogenous to service scale. 3. Construct mismatch in Capacidade_Operacional: Operational capacity is built from solid-waste/public-cleaning employees and vehicles (Empregados and Veículos for RDO/RPU), not water/sewage staff, yet is entered as a regressor in the water and sewage models. 4. Sample attrition and outlier dropping: Minas Gerais has 853 municipalities, boxplot outlier removal reduced the descriptive sample to N = 574 (N = 456 for PMSB, N = 471 for PPSB), and listwise deletion reduced the regression sample to N = 391; furthermore, SNIS self-reporting is itself correlated with municipal capacity. 5. Borderline 10% significance stars: In Model 3 (solid waste, Atend_RDO), the authors treat p = 0.078 (Capacidade_Tecnica) and p = 0.055 (Capacidade_Politica) as supporting their hypotheses at the 10% level (*), whereas both are null at conventional p < 0.05.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional observational municipal-level quantitative study using Exploratory Factor Analysis (PCA with varimax rotation) and OLS multiple linear regression with White heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (plus bivariate Chi-square and ANOVA tests by municipal population size), using 2018 SNIS and 2017 IBGE data.
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Municipalities in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil: N = 574 municipalities in descriptive/exploratory sample after boxplot outlier removal (with N = 530 for Tecnico_Esgoto, N = 471 for PPSB, and N = 456 for PMSB; Table 2, PDF p. 19), and N = 391 municipalities with complete data in the primary OLS multiple linear regression models (PDF p. 22; Table 4, PDF p. 23).
